2016-July-03
Quick Rundown:
------------------------
The good: Gameplay mechanics are solid, if a bit simplistic.
The bad: Exceptionally difficult to find others to play with.
Verdict: A hopeful 6/10 in its current state. Fun for a quick romp but disappointed about not having enough friends to play with. Interface, matchmaking, and netcode need a few tweaks.
Potential: 8/10 with a solid-buy recommendation if matchmaking gets an overhaul. Once the multiplayer community gets up and running,
-
Built on the Unity engine, Kill to Collect is a 1-4 player skill based top-down brawler of sorts with an 80's neon/cyberpunk theme and music to match. KTC is an action-oriented tactical brawler with a good degree of challenge and a high skill ceiling, button-mashing wont serve you well here. The basic premise of the game is that you (and a group of friends if lucky) delve into futuristic / dystopian slums with the goal of hunting a bounty (boss) and clearing the place of its riff-raff. Along the way you will find one-time use heals, shields, powerups, deployables (such as mines), and even swappable ammo-based weapons as you make your way through the floor. At the end of each section you are allowed to take a break in the rec-room and spend some of the chips you've accumulated to buy yourself permanent upgrades, replenish your health and ammo, stock up on items, or purchase a different secondary weapon.
There are 4 character classes in Kill to Collect, and while they all feel fairly similar, they do each have their own strengths and weaknesses from being a slow-ish and tanky shotgun brawler with a Juggernaut-like ultimate ability to a crazy shock-staffed, jetpack-wearing, turret deploying crowd control character. Each of the four different classes has their own set of abilities that work better or worse against certain enemy types in a Gauntlet-esq manner, but are still similar enough so as to not become obsolete when used in solo play. Due to the nature of these differences, the game really shines in multiplayer when you can combine these with allied abilities, but thanks to a small playerbase, finding a multiplayer game can be quite difficult.
The brawler-esq 3rd person top-down combat in KTC is broken down into an exceptionally simple set of attacks and moves; A basic attack, a special knock-down attack on a cooldown, an ultimate ability on a kill-based cooldown, and a limited ammo-based interchangeable weapon. Additionally each character has their own dodge ability from a steerable and fast moving jetpack that can be used to knock enemies aside, to a short ranged blink which can teleport to the other side of an enemy (admittedly a bit fiddly), and of course a fairly plain-jane dodgeroll too. The special attacks for each character feel similar, but do impart different effects on the enemy from armor breaking debuffs which make an enemy take more damage on their next hit to stuns and knockdowns which in some cases are only effective against certain types of enemies.
An upgrade/unlock system of sorts is in place, but its incredibly simple and very linear. Basically, as you collect bounties (score) from playing and beating levels, you unlock skins and new loadouts which allow you to change the two starting items that you begin the game with. Loadouts are a fairly minor thing overall, but do influence the early-game. Unlocks for golden weapon skins are attained by completing objectives based around using those weapons, but these golden weapons dont appear to have any gameplay impact, nor can these skins be disabled.. so any uniqueness of each weapon's texture/color is basically lost after you've completed its associated task. Pieces Interactive definitely could have done a bit more with this system while maintaining balance and keeping power-creep at bay. In its current state these systems feel a little under-developed and disappointing. Collected bounty is basically just a measurement of how much you've played.. a global score of sorts; you dont use it to buy unlocks, loadouts, or skins, they just get unlocked when you reach a totally linear and arbitrary amount.
Ultimately the crippling factor for Kill to Collect at the moment is that its missing its multiplayer community. Its a solid game which needs more players. They've done a really good job with core fighting mechanics and balancing, and aside from a bit of peer-to-peer lag, the multiplayer mechanics feel pretty good. Revive systems are in place to keep the flow of the game going and reward players who are good by keeping them revived or bringing them back after locating or beating special rooms. The increased number of enemies in multiplayer offer additional challenge, and there is plenty of chaos and opportunity to work together to make some fun and exciting things happen based on the game's various knock-back mechanics and ragdoll-physics. If there was a stronger multiplayer community that allowed you to find games whenever you wanted, I feel that this game would offer a significantly higher value for its cost. As it stands, I cannot recommend Kill to Collect at its full price unless you absolutely love this type of game, or have a group of friends to play with. If you enjoyed games like Spiral Knights, then this will probably be something you will find familiar and appealing. Though due to the simple combat mechanics and lack of complex interactions in single player the game can feel a tad samey after awhile, having a friend or two to play with may make all the difference.
Final thoughts: Pieces Interactive needs to step up their marketing department and get people playing their game. Its a good title that gets put down all too quickly due to the lack of community to engage with. Single player delivers a couple of hours of good challenge while multiplayer offers some exciting, funny, and tensely rewarding moments. Sadly unless your friends own the game, theres almost no chance of finding a random multiplayer pick-up game to join at this time. Kill to Collect is a good game that Id enjoy playing with friends and with random people, sadly it will be difficult to convince friends to buy without an active multiplayer community and with such a flawed matchmaking system in place.
Pros:
- Good visceral core combat mechanics.
- Decent player character and enemy variety.
- Has single player modes, offers a good challenge.
- The kind of game that truly shines when played with friends.
Cons:
- No multiplayer community as of 2016-07-03. Finding a random MP game is impossible.
- Cant do anything but sit at the host screen while you wait for someone to join.
- Host-side hit detection means that players will feel some lag / sluggish feedback.
- Cannot disable autoaim for keyboard and mouse controls.
- Maxes out GPU clocks, even when minimized and vsynced. (Radeon 7850)
- Title is no longer receiving support. No contact or fixes from developers 6+ months.

I had to click the mouse. The eyeball in the background is the main character's; furthermore, when you move your move around the eyeball follows you.
Graphics: 10/10 Beautiful.
Plot: The protagonist awakens and embarks on a mission. She is looking for something or perhaps someone important. The subject of her grandfather always comes up. She is trying to finish what her grandfather was investing in. I have not yet played enough but I am only explaining the main points here.
Genre: Space yet very unique and different.
Gameplay: Nothing new that I haven't seen before that is pretty solid; however, I wish the game had a bit more interactions in the world. I got to shoot my gun once after a long time of walking; furthermore, I eventually got the option to shout saying Hello? or Anyone Home? for a while at some point. WOW THIS IS FABULOUS. Bright colors, techno mariachi music, and beautiful, BEAUTIFUL 2D platformer handling. And sometimes I get to be a chicken. It is everything I didn't know I wanted in a Metroidvania.
Before I bought it, I thought this was a go-to-the-right-beat-em-up like the arcade version of TMNT or THE SIMPSONS. But then it came up during a lookup of Metroidvanias and I had a closer look. I still wasn't quite sure if it was the game for me. THEN there was a sale--get the Super Turbo Championship Edition, Gold Edition, AND soundtrack for $6. I couldn't pass up the deal.
Since the Super Turbo version looked to be the more "complete" version of the game, I deleted the Gold version and started my GUACAMELEE journey.
This game does a ton of things right. Checkpoints are generous. The beat 'em up sections are fun to complete, even when playing on a keyboard. Miss a platform jump (in a series of them over water), and instead of going back to a last checkpoint, you go to the last bit of solid ground you stood on. THANK YOU, GUACAMELEE, FOR RESPECTING MY TIME.
I groused at first about the lack of double-jump, but in the end, I was glad they made me use the Rooster Punch so often, because then I discovered its versatility. Then when I did get double jump, I found myself using it differently.
Within hours, I was zipping across the neon landscape like a champ, goat-jumping off walls while switching dimensions and punching skeletons in the face like a stud. THAT'S what I play platformers for.
The abilities upgrade system is a little weak -- at times it was hard to see how spending pesos improved said abilities--
As a kid, I fell in love with Castlevania: Symphony of the Night for its dark-yet-fun horror-gothic vibe. I grew up with the Donkey Kong Country games. I've played nearly all the Nifflas platformers, which have a chill mystique. GUACAMELEE has the wonderful quality of movement of ALL those games PLUS a zesty feast for your eyes and ears, the most festive, fun platformer I've played in a L O N G time.
Come for the platforming, stay for the art. And chicken.
It's a masterpiece.

However, Sophia needs to find a centaur that will forge the weapon that will defeat the evil entity. And while trying to find a way to stop the war (though you'll see that the twist in the end that will solve everything).
If the plot is well-written and can be played without any prior knowledge, I found it just disappointing not to have the whole story on Steam, even if Big Fish promised to release the beginning under the form of a bundle. You're missing all Sophia's background and journey to what she is now.
The gameplay is quite the standard one: find items to use after, solve puzzles and clear hidden objects scenes (whether in the form of objects to use, of a shaped list or a list of words). What is cool here is that these scenes can be incorporated into the story (for example, being searching for something for the healer). The puzzles are easy. However, I've a small complaint: sometimes, I couldn't really find what to do because I've missed an item somewhere.
The graphics are really good, colorful and sad in the same time. The soundtrack was good too.
The fact that is a collector's edition is also interesting: aside from the usual bonus, you have a garden where you can play minigames and where you can make plants grow!
So yeah, Awakening: The Redleaf Forest is a very good purchase. You would be crazy to miss it if you're a casual adventure gamer. And the full price is justified. Now, I'm just waiting for Big Fish to keep their promise to release the rest on Steam.

I'm not going to blame a game developer from trying to sell their game on Steam, even if it is available online to play for free.  For fans who want to support them and be able to download the game for their personal long-term use, it can be a win-win for everyone, even if it can come off as being chintzy.  However, this game wasn't worth porting.  I have no idea how it plays on the original site, but it's broken through Steam.
Like many others, I started getting stuck only a few levels into the game because it's simply absolute rubbish.  You go against a CPU and try to launch the best units and spells in order to wipe out their castle before your own is destroyed.  The first 2 or so levels work out well enough, since you have almost no options and can't help winning, but as you start being able to upgrade your units the game shows how poorly it was designed.  The CPU spawns enemies and spells faster than you do, making it so you have to play flawlessly in both unit deployment and which units get upgraded between levels.  A well designed version of this game would allow the player to upgrade units at their discretion and play to their own style, and if you got stuck you could grind earlier levels for more experience/gold to upgrade and make your way through.  In this game you can't replay earlier levels (like you'd really want to anyways) to do that.  You can reset your upgrades, but by the point you have to do that you're more or less done playing this turd anyways.
Despite these flaws, I actually figured out a rather simple method to make progress in the game.  Instead of balancing upgrades, just burn them all into a single unit (I went with the first one) 'til it's maxed out, then max out fire, and keep maxing upgrades out.  All units recharge at the same rate regardless of what level they're upgraded to, so there's no reason to not focus on only one.  Same goes with the spells.  I would have been able to beat the game this way except for one simple thing.  Before I had even played for 30 minutes, having about 5-6 levels left to beat, the UI started glitching out on me.  I would try to spawn a unit and all of the icons disappeared and the game stopped working.  Disfunctionality like that should necessitate a game being removed from Steam, since they have had months to fix this gaping flaw, but you can still buy this hunk of junk (like anyone would with this abyssmal rating - I doubt anyone will even read this review for that reason).  The good news is that if you do buy this the game will break itself in under 2 hours and you can get a full refund.  If you got it for free like I did, you'll play it out to get your cards and remove this game to never play it again.  I won't even complete the badge for this game because I don't want it fouling up my profile anymore than it already has.  If you buy a game with this low a rating, period, you have only yourself to blame because you've been warned.

I bought this game awhile ago and never really got to playing it. It started it, but the art didn’t really appeal to me. However, now that I actually gave it a chance I’ve gotta say this is a solid visual novel. It has romance, mystery and science fiction and a story that makes up for the less polished artwork.
The characters that you can romance each have their own backstories and reasons doing what they are doing. They have a variety of types: sweet and innocent, lecherous and clever, genteel and polite, rough and tumble and the boy next door. There are good endings and bad endings. There is a final ending, but you have to complete all other routes to get there.
It’s pretty typical on gameplay. It does have the added twist of a fairly simple puzzle you have to do before you pick your answer. Once you’ve picked an answer you can skip the puzzle and pick that answer the next time you play through without having to redo that puzzle. This is seriously one of the most severely underrated visual novels I've ever seen. The writing is strong, the characters are flawed and complex yet still likeable, and the sci-fi/mystery aspect is super interesting, putting a nice twist on the typical otome genre. I really enjoyed playing each route to unravel the larger overall story. I also really liked how the protagonist herself gets a fleshed out character and backstory instead of being a completely blank slate; she has so much personality, I felt like I was unraveling her story too. The true ending was strong and it felt like everything got wrapped up nicely. Date Warp is a very enjoyable game overall and its pacing and length feels just right -- it's not super short but it doesn't feel like it drags on and on forever either -- which I think is pretty hard to do in dating sims like this where you need to play each route to get the full story. On a more minor note, I thought the music in the game was very good too, it was very fitting and atmospheric throughout. I like how it was mostly electronic, it really added to the sci-fi vibe of the game.
I also learned that the version of this game on steam is the updated silver edition or whatever with  some new writing and an updated epilogue - I think that it's really cool for the developers to care enough to go back and do that for an older game of theirs. Achievements and trading cards are also a nice bonus.
The only real downside is perhaps some of the CG art for events looks a little rough around the edges, and the fact that you need to complete puzzles to select your dialogue options is kind of weird, but neither is a big detractor by a long shot. Thankfully, after you've already done a puzzle for one dialogue option, you'll never have to do it again -- a nice anti-frustration feature. The art overall is solid and the game is fantastic. It's another strong title from Hanako Games that hasn't gotten nearly as much attention as their other works.

The game looks very decent and makes excellent use of its dynamic camera to render its 3D environments in the most appropriate angle with proper depth of field, while retaining that classic adventure game feel. It's a slight innovation that gives it a particularly enjoyable uniqueness.
Perhaps somewhat strangely for a title of this genre, it is obviously intended to be controlled with a gamepad, and surprisingly this works remarkably well for the most part. Only using the inventory proves slightly cumbersome, until you get used it, and there's always the more traditional mouse and keyboard alternative for the die-hards.
The games' writing, humour and dialogue are dosed just right, abundantly breaking the 4th wall. The relatively vague story and inept main protagonist may certainly not break new grounds but are nevertheless entertaining. Laid-back and logical puzzles reward exploration and trying funny ideas without punishing players with failure or death, all very fitting with the theme.
Excellent soundtrack.
A very polished but unquestionably very short experience with about 3 hours worth of quality content at most. It ends a bit abruptly, making the overall plot feel very aimless and giving the impression of an incomplete slice of a larger, unfinished whole.
For this reason alone I would recommend getting it on sale, but otherwise highly recommended. Here's hoping for a proper sequel!

You like a playful point-and-click adventure which doesn't take itself too seriously... but are happy with a short play time of 2-4 hours.
To be very frank (English... fnarr fnarr) - My one (and only) quibble with this game is its duration. With a lifespan 2-4 hours, it's just too little bang-for-your-buck to be able to comfortably recommend without mentioning this caveat.
Hats off to the team though, what's there is a promising, very polished rival to the Lucas Arts point-and-click adventures... if funnier. The graphics are superb and the puzzles felt nicely balanced to be tricky without becoming too laborious. They were also intuitive enough so that the solution made sense... meaning you don't have those frustrating moments of "oh come on! How the frick was I supposed to figure out that you needed a thong and a dart to lock-pick a cupboard!?" (true story). Your inventory is (graciously) kept quite lean as well, so you're not lugging around 20 objects which you torturously try and combine with every item you come across whilst shedding an exasperated tear.
The characters are great. And whilst the self-deprecating "this is a poorly-researched, cheap game" jokes felt a little strained, the humour is fantastic and made for several laugh out loud moments. Excellent cultural references (the Robot Wars one really tickled me), good interactions between the characters and some cracking one-liners to be had.
Whilst I'm generally indifferent to achievements: They make for some clever side-puzzles for you to figure out, which can help to squeeze a bit more life out of this title.
So don't get me wrong; the game's good fun... it just comes with the big, fat caveat of "it's very short".

Unfair Jousting Fair is a fun and simple game
The controls are very simple. You move left or right to balance yourself on your unicycle. You move up and down to adjust your weapon. That's it!
The aim of the game is to hit your opponent with the end of your weapon, and avoid having the same happen to you. It's pretty fun due to a few of the randomizers that go on. As you play more, you unlock weapons. Every round, you have a random chance to get any of the weapons you've unlocked, which makes for some interesting battles as you might find yourself with a short rolling pin, yet your opponent will have a long rake.
You can also hit chickens at your enemy, or have to climb up a ramp. Stuff like that keeps the game interesting. There are also a few features which make for some funny and intense moments. If your two weapons clash, they will bounce back, and if your heads touch, your characters will kiss and bounce back.
Keep in mind at the moment it's strictly local multiplayer. No online, and no singleplayer. There isn't too much to keep you playing the game for long after maybe half an hour. Although it's a fun little game that you could pick up for a few rounds every now and again when your friend is over!

I played this game at Madrid Games Week and it's hilarious! I mean, you can joust on snails and as the devs explained to me, that's even historically accurate (in a twisted kind of way)! The fact that rounds are kept short gives it that lovely "just one more time"-quality. The music supports the mood nicely and there's lots of little unlockables that add variety. The controls reminded me of qwop, you get that same sense of amusement at your own clumsiness, yet they evidently can be mastered; it must be cool to see two experienced players have a go.
Would love to see this game come to other platforms as it is perfect to add variety to my and my friends' local multiplayer rotation.

When you look at Unfair Jousting Fair you see a game that clearly has no problems be wacky. You are after all competing in a jousting competition riding unicycles while brandishing random weapons which include rakes and floor lamps. This total randomness is the best part of the game. It's hard not to chuckle at some of the situations that transpire in the game.
The controls are kind of hard to get a handle on. I think this was somewhat done on purpose. While you will get better at the controls with practice, you will likely never master them. In order to move forward you kind of have to rock back and forth which will sometimes lead to you falling down before you even reach your opponent. This is sometimes funny but can also be frustrating as well.
The combat is pretty simple as you are pretty much just trying to hit the other player. The longer weapons seem to have an advantage since you can reach the other player before they can even touch you.
I would like to point out that Unfair Jousting Fair is solely a local multiplayer game. You need a second player and at this time there is no online mode so you need to find another person to play the local multiplayer with.
The biggest issue with the game is the longevity. After about fifteen to twenty minutes Unfair Jousting Fair get a little boring. At least for me it is the type of game that I would come back to every so often but I know some players could be sick of the game after that amount of time.
If the game's concept interests you, you have someone else to play the game with and you don't quickly tire of games I think you will enjoy Unfair Jousting Fair. If not Unfair Jousting Fair may not be for you.
Note: I received a free review copy of the game from the developer.

Kill to collect is a co-op multiplayer (or singleplayer) experience with cyberpunk attributes and some rather interesting and unique level design implemented into each mission of the game. The game is rather fast paced, and focuses upon combat more than anything else in the game.
Apparently the game is tagged as Rogue-lite/like which I don't 100% agree with. The game has some elements of this sort of genre but I wouldn't tag it as that, I know that the tags are made from the most popular by steam users but it's just something I had to say.
Kill to collect is a fast paced, cyberpunk themed addicting game that concentrates solely on the combat but does well with presenting everything else as well. The combat is elegantly designed which has had a lot of thought and process gone through how every move works.  The combat combines fast paced with quick thinking and strategic play in order to outsmart your enemies and kill them easier, the game doesn't rely on how fast you can spam the attack button which is a very good think to have in a game like this. Because who really likes mashing a button to attack with bare minimum combat system? The environment of the game itself is well thought out and presented, you can actually use this to your advantage to kill your enemies easier and quicker.
With this sort of combat system, it won't be easy. The game seems to take a lot of skill (especially in single player as all the enemies will walk towards you) which definitely would require you to be able to talk to your other teammates in order to get good at the game and be more strategic with your attacks.
The difficulty of this game comes from the enemies that you encounter throughout each of the rooms that you go in before you get to the main bounty. Some of the enemies are plain and simple, but as you get further into the game the enemies start to develop a more interesting and challenging mechanics that will make the game a bit more harder for you. But the way that they do this isn't like other games similar to this, they are not given tons of health, damage or defense boosts in order to make it difficult. Both you and the enemies die in a couple of hits, this makes the combat system more difficult and makes you focus more upon timing, dodging and careful positioning of each of your attacks in order to make them the fullest and most effective that they can be. You will know when you have made a mistake, because you will be punished harshly with either death or low health.
The progression with each of the characters that you play as needs a bit more work. It does feel a bit meh and doesn't really feel like you are progressing in the sort of way that you would expect to do throughout the game. I feel like even though there are only 4 characters in the game, that they could of expanded a bit more on the sort of characters that you could of played as. For me, the first hour of the game was me testing out the characters and what sort of combat style there was, and for me personally they all just felt dull and not really that interesting all together. A few more characters in this game would add to a bit more variety to the game I think.
The game's graphics are so bright and vibrant, I feel like it brings the game to life and really helps with the fast paced that the game is going for. With the cyberpunk theme it really hits the nail on the head for the game all together. With all the characters being fairly bright and colourful, as well as the walls and everything else in the game it really sets a high standard for the game if you're just watching the trailer to see if you like this game or not.
+ Elegant combat system

- Needs more characters to vary it a bit

Date Warp is a short game with an intriguing plotline. I finished all the routes in a couple of hours, though I skipped a lot of the shared dialogue—there's a lot shared between routes, since the central plot remains the same. That's one thing that bugged me a bit, though that's common in visual novels, I've noticed. However, having played Magical Diary, a later Hanako Games title, I can say the way the repeated dialogue was handled in that felt a bit less dry, since there were more ways to explore in the game.
Some of the art was better than other examples...Linds and Nathaniel tended to look good, but the art was iffy in a lot of the CGs, and some of the reactions for characters looked off. I don't mind art as much as other people, so this wasn't a big deal for me, nor was I bothered by the lack of voicing.
You choose your options with a puzzle game where you build a circuit through some twisted wire to build a path to the option you want to select. I liked this, especially since you can skip the puzzle if you've already solved it for an option that you want to select again.
The way the plotlines culminate in the final playthrough was quite good, but I feel like there was a lot that could've been done better, such as it leaving me wanting to know more about some of the characters and the universe, but in a sort of empty way, not in an excited one.
Overall, this is a good game, but painfully short and with too much repeated (though, if you play through the whole game, you could argue that's part of the point with regard to the plot.) It left me wanting more than it could give me.
I bought it for 75% off, leaving it below $3, which I thought was worth it. Would I pay $9.99 for it? No. Is it still worth playing? Yeah, if you don't pay $9.99 for it!
I'd give it a 7/10, maybe a 6.0 to 6.5 if I'm being harsh.

This is probably one of my favourite visual novels yet. The scenario is really well put together - the sci-fi elements make internal sense as far as I can see, and the visual novel format has been used to its full potential.
The characters all start out a little like stereotypes (you have Linds, the mad scientist, Alben the emo trash, Bradley the boy next door etc) but over the course of the routes they all become decent characters with multiple layers. I really love how the story-telling works between routes - there's a clear consistency to it. The protagonist acts based on the information she has at hand, and although a lot of the text is repeated through routes it has been altered where need be. I know this seems like a weird thing to fangirl about, but I appreciate good writing and this game has it.
I love how the endings (excluding the True End) cannot clearly be defined as 'good' or 'bad'. Some of them pack quite the emotional punch. Others are more of a cliff-hanger...Some are definitely stronger than others, as a handful feel rather rushed.
I really enjoyed the puzzle mechanic, it made the choices seem far more significant and made me feel more involved in the story. It's a clever little technique I haven't seen before.
The art is not the best, you can see that in the screenshots, but the story was good enough that I could overlook it. The whole game feels dated, but in a weirdly charming way.
If you enjoy visual novels, this is a must read.

Homebrew is a game where you dream, plan and create your very own vehicle. Do not be fooled by the cartoon graphics. This game includes a very steep learning curve in order to design a car. For example, for a basic car you will need 4 wheel hubs, 8 metal pipes, a bucket seat, an engine, a fuel tank, a smooth box, a toggle box and a 12V battery. Also including that you need to tune the car and connect wires together to make each part of the car work. The learning curve may be very difficult and challenging but after a few hours of getting used to it and remaking the car over and over again, you get used to it and can eventually learn what to do off by heart although the more complex things you want to make, the more difficult the tuning will be.
In this game you can create anything that is mobile to your dreams. Could be a jetpack. Could be a go-kart. Could be a ground roller coaster. Aeroplane. Anything. The best thing is that you can share your creations amongst your friends as well as test them for yourself in a roughly 40km Area of an island. This gives you plenty of room and places such as a runway, race course, sea and everything. This game is amazing. If you’re not a fan of taking a few hours to learn something to build amazing things, I do not recommend this game for you but if you don’t mind, this game is the game for you.

Echo is an interesting game where every “cycle” (when the lights turn on and off) AI copies of yourself adopt actions from the previous cycle meaning you must get crafty with what you do to achieve objectives scattered across large levels. Essentially the game is you walking from room to room being given exposition about the world and characters and then dealing with your clone counterparts. You’ll learn tiny details about every mechanic giving them more utility uses which makes the game feel more organic as you learn how best to deal with your doppelgangers. I should also mention this game has a selection of collectable, secrets and alternate game modes which should help alleviate the games six-hour runtime.
What I will say is that I feel as if the game does not evolve that much as you play it. While there are some interesting mechanics which I don’t want to spoil introduced later, it felt like the game didn’t change all that much between start and finish. Most times I felt that each room was like the last one, this doesn’t kill the experience, but I felt like there had to be more than what was on display. Also on another note the story is… ummm. Well not great but not bad either, it tries a little too hard focusing on a plot about intrigue, guilt and sacrifice while not really achieving much between the only two characters in the game En and the hundred-year-old AI London. The story does do an excellent job exploring the strange mythos and utility of The Palace.
All in all, I suggest you buy Echo. It’s weird enough to leave a lasting impression on you, and there aren’t many games that can boast mechanics where the AI learns and reacts to your actions.

ECHO is a great game that managed for me what only 2 or 3 games could pull off within the last years: It put the studio behind it on my "buy on release, those people deserve it!"-list!
It´s a stealth/action-game with unique mechanics. The Echos copy your behavior after the regulary occuring resets. The aim is not to kill them, but to reach objectives despite them. Since they get reset regulary, the Echos are endless enemies that adapt and do to you, what you do to them. And yes, that includes instakilling you from behind, shooting and playing the harp! UPDATING AFTER BEATING THE GAME:
While it can be great fun to play, oversized maps and shoddy controls make it hard to love.
I gave it a 3/5
Visuals are awesome
Music is awesome
Concept is awesome
Reliability is awesome
Scale is great, but too large for the content
Controls are pretty good, but the autotarget is worthless
Enemy variety is pretty good, but most enemies have one of 5 attacks with different animations.
The targeting system constantly switches targets on you, so you need to do it manually
There are maybe two missions per area, with no side missions or interesting deviations from the plot.
The story is purely there to lead you from point A to point B
The prerecorded scenes look like they were hashed together at the last minute
Basically, you go from territory to territory, killing monsters, destroying lairs (which spawn monsters) and upgrading a central city until you're told it's high enough.  Then you are given a different mission.  Most of these are rinse and repeat in a different area, but there are a few odd jobs where you switch control to a hunter or wizard or warlord.  I think I enjoyed maybe two of them.
I liked the game, but I think the biggest problem with it was... I didn't feel like a giant fire-breathing harbinger of death.  A good half the enemies were bigger than me, and most of them were few and far between.  The battle scenes were all far smaller than you'll see in the screenshot, and the maps were too empty for me to feel anything.
Is it a great game?  Nah, but I'd definitely pick it up for 6 bucks and give it a try if I were you.  It's a really cool concept, and I hope someone else does it better next time around.

Guacamelee! is a action platformer with combo-based melee combat and exploration elements. You play as Juan, a farmer who gains superpowers after finding a mysterious luchador mask. You fight through throngs of enemies in a Mexican-inspired setting on your quest to rescue El Presidente's kidnapped daughter.
Super Turbo Championship Edition is rather pointless (and frankly greedy) rerelease of the game with rebalanced encounters, some new content and a poorly implemented new mechanic. In hindsight I should have just played the earlier Gold Edition instead of buying this one. Rather annoyingly there's no discount anymore for upgrading from the Gold Edition and you have to pay the full price for this one even if you own the earlier release .
The game has a strong visual style that fits the theme well. Unfortunately the visuals leave a lot to be desired on a technical level. A lot of the artwork is rather poorly done and the animations in particular are terrible. Also, the game does not properly support 16:10 resolutions.
The game also suffers from rather heavy tearing on my system. Enabling vsync will fix the issue but leads to extremely nearly unplayable controller lag.
The sound effects are decent enough although there seemed to be issues with the timings of some sounds. The music is well done if rather repetitive and fits the theme well. There's no real voice acting.
The game plays like a fairly typical metroidvania with combo-based melee combat. You explore the maps and unlock special powers that let you progress to new areas. These powers are pretty standard from wall climbing and double jumping to various attack moves that let you break through special color-coded walls.
You also gain the power to switch between the land of the dead and the land of the living, although nothing particularly inventive is done with this ability. In practice it's mainly used for a lot of rather repetitive and tedious platforming sections.
My early impressions of the combat were quite positive. Chaining the combos is fun and the combat flows quite well. Unfortunately as you progress the game keeps adding more and more gimmicky elements that mess up the core gameplay. Having to constantly break enemy shields and switch between the land of the dead/living just breaks the flow and makes the combat lot less enjoyable.
Way too much of the combat also takes place in small closed-off arenas. I certainly felt that this was a rather baffling design choice in a metroidvania game and would have preferred more open-ended encounters.
I found the game pretty easy on normal difficulty, although this will be heavily dependant on your ability to pull of combos and your platforming skills. The final area is certainly a big step up in difficulty and some of the optional puzzles and areas are quite a bit harder too.
The controls are pretty solid on a gamepad. Some moves can feel slightly imprecise, however.
The story is very basic and cliché. The writing is pretty terrible too and the jokes in particular are extremely cringeworthy. I felt that much more could have been done with the Mexican theme.
Overall the game is fairly polished and I didn't encounter any major bugs.
Personally I found Guacamelee! a somewhat disappointing game. The core gameplay is solid enough, but the game introduces way too many poorly implemented powers and gimmicky enemies that end up making the combat lot less fun. The writing is pretty terrible too and the exploration aspects are not particularly satisfying. It's not a terrible game by any means, but I still didn't find it enjoyable enough to recommend.
It took me little under 6 hours to play through the game on normal. I didn't bother with most optional areas, just completed the main story.

ECHO is a game that respects its player's intelligence. Exposition and world-building are woven directly into En and London's emotion-filled dialogue without it ever sounding unnatural. In a way it makes it more difficult to put the pieces together since they are often thrown in for context when the two argue without being clearly explained, but it doesn't take away from the feeling of a big and rich Sci-Fi universe that is out there.
The story however isn't about that universe, it's a very focused and character-driven narrative, and I have to give huge props to the British VAs behind En and London. There is banter, there is gut-wrenching sorrow, and there is just so much character development that feels genuine and earned rather than tacky.
Speaking of VAs, sound design is spot on. The game doesn't have a soundtrack that's meant to be listened to by itself as such, rather it has great ambient music and a ton of uniqe sound ques linked to gameplay, which combine for a very strong audio experience. The blackout cycles especially are very impactful in their sound design.
Aesthetic is another strong suit of the game. The clash of New and Old is used to great effect. The Palace looks magnificent and the Sci-Fi technology it is filled with both in the forms of En and her clones, as well as the Palace's own machinations, are absolutely stunning. The level of detail too is impressive, even if you see a lot reused assets it is clear that every one of these assets has been used to its full potential and doesn't feel out of place. Unreal Engine does its work prefectly and the graphics look beautiful, but the design of the Palace and its many fantastical mechanisms are what makes you want to explore it. It inspires a true sense of splendor and awe through its vastness. You really feel like an ant in the house of aristocrats.
Gameplay is perhaps where the game is strongest and weakest at the same time. I won't explain the mechanics, I'll take it for granted you watched the gameplay trailer, it explains itself pretty clearly. Problem is that it feels like the game uses up most of its potential early on and doesn't introduce enough new mechanics to keep you interested. It is very much a game that relies on its replayability, but while very fun and novel at first its easy to burn yourself out to a point where it feels like the game overstays its welcome even for how short it is. It introduces a new enemy type towards the end of game very abruptly and throws a ton of them at you before you have a chance to get used to them, which doesn't really feel great since the only way to get used to them involves being killed by them (a lot), and then it's suddenly The End before you know it. The first few hours are definitely the better part of the experience.
That being said, the game is built for replayability with different approaches. If you want it to be a stealth game, it will be a stealth game with sneaky enemies and tons of mechanics allowing you to outsmart them. If you want it be an action game, it will be an action game where engaging enemies strategically and managing your resources well will be the key to survival. Best part is of course that by mixing up your gameplay between balckout cycles allows you to take full advantage of these mechanics, wether you decide to alternate stealth and action gameplay between day cycles, or to play cautiosly in the light and balls to the walls during the dark. The blackouts come faster when you have enemies chasing you or have killed too many. This works really well to balance the gameplay and it always feels like the balckout comes at just the right moment to save your sorry♥♥♥♥♥
In conclusion: ECHO has a very unique character to it with beautiful audio-visual design, strong and interesting characters, and novel gameplay mechanic that introduces a lot of replay value. It is an indie game made with heart and artistic vision and definitely provides enough value to justify its price tag. Just don't overdo it or you might get bored of it too quickly.

After a few hours of play.... Over 100.... I can finally do an overall review of FTO!
Fantasy Tales Online
Free to Play w/Cashshop
No pay to win elements, Cashshop only adds items with no advantage to combat.
FIrstly I will add that this of course as you know Early Access. Now we have all grown tired of these games because we tend to expect more than we should. I will tell you that this game is very smooth and polished for an early access. The only issue is amount of content at this point. The dev team is small and is trying hard to add content constantly, however after about 2 weeks you will done with it all. That being said that doesnt mean you wont have anything to do! Now for my review
Graphics 7/10- If you like 2d Games(zelda style) this is the game for you and shoul be a 10/10, however because this is an older style of graphics I have to round it down a bit to be fair :). Overall pleasing to the eye and simple. The devs have done a great job adding detail to the maps.
Sound- 7/10- Game has charming music and very simple sound effects. Not advanced and not so dull you want to mute it. The usual 2d mmo music style.
Controls- 8/10- Typical MMO controls WASD and Number skill hotkeys etc. The controls are awesome and when refined will be a solid 10/10 for a 2d MMO.
Gameplay- 6/10- The gameplay is smooth as butter and the physics between you and the world are great. Not alot of bugs and the game runs at a solid 60 FPS on even the simplest of computers. Whip out those old Laptops because this game can play on it! The combat is fun and simple but can become VERY grindy as the higher lvl need EXTREME amounts of XP. However this is done on purpose by devs to make the (end Game) Lvls be much harder to obtain while any player can hit the soft lvl cap with ease. This game is a PURE Grindfest as it stands right now which I do not think is the direction the devs want to go, however because the 4 or 5 best pieces of equipment are EXTREMELY rare random drops in 1 or 2 raids (Instanced mazes of rooms with repeated mobs and a final boss) that means the ONLY way to compete for dps etc is to grind for those weapons which I cannot lie gets very stamina draining and boring... IF you can deal with the grinding for a few pieces of equipment than this will not bother you that much. Also currently there is NO PVP in this game.. it is on the to do list of the devs but doesnt seem to be a priority which is causing some frustration with alot of players because this is a great way to add unlimited gameplay to the servers.
Community- 5/10- This game has great potential to have a great community however the player count is very low ATM. The devs are very busy but they do try and monitor the forum and in game chat often. The devs listen to the members and try to move the game in the direction off of player input. There are a few bad apples in the game as far as players go but you tend to ignore them. Once people start playing this score has alot of potential to climb higher.
Summary: Overall this is a great little game that just needs its moment to shine. Once it gets some spotlight the servers will fill up fast! Right now they sit at anywhere between 25 to 100 players at any given time. As far as 2d Free to play MMORPGs go I consider this one of the best! I play alot on US Server 1 Diamond Shard so hope on in and gives this great game a try! Its FREE!!!

After 45 hours in this game I feel I've played enough to write an honest review.
This game is mediocre in most respects, but does one thing very, very well. The combat is extremely well designed. It's fast paced, but also greatly rewards stategic play, quick thinking, and using your environment to your advantage. It's fun, but also takes a great amount of skill. The enemies are challenging, but their attacks are almost always avoidable (with only a few rare exceptions). The difficulty comes from the enemies having interesting and challenging mechanics, not by simply giving them lots of health and damage. Both the player and the enemies die in only a few hits, making the combat about very careful positioning, timing, dodging and strategy, rather than it being about DPS, armor, gear or any stats. In Kill to Collect, when you die, it's because you made a mistake.
The combat is so good, that despite most other aspects of the game being nothing special, I consider this to be one of the best games I've played in a long time. It's hard to adequately describe it in words or showcase in a video, you pretty much have to play to understand.
Other things I like about this game:
- The four characters all feel significantly different from each other in their style of fighting, but are all fairly balanced.
- It has co-op, while almost every other rogue-lite does not.
- Basically no time wasted on dialogue, travelling, sorting items, or anything else boring. You will spend 90% of your time fighting.
- The music is good and suits the atmosphere of the game very well, although like all game music, you'll probably want to turn it off eventually.
- Daily challenge missions with a leaderboard let you compete with others for daily high scores.
Things I do not like:
- The aim assist. Although necessary for this type of combat (especially for newer players), sometimes it can be a major liability. At this point, I'd say at least a third of the damage I take is aim assist related, and that's a conservative estimate. There needs to be a button to toggle it on or off.
- The player base is very small. It can be very hard to find people to play co-op with using the in-game matchmaking. If you want to play co-op, you'll need to have friends, or add people off the forums.
- The hit detection is host-side, rather than client-side, making it difficult to play with friends from another region due to lag.
- Currently, due to how the difficulty scales, co-op can be significantly harder than solo.
- The "Hard" difficulty is exactly the same as normal, except you get only 1 HP. It's definitely hard, but it feels also a bit lazy and causes some balance issues. This problem is not as bad as it sounds though, because most players can't beat normal difficulty.
- A couple combinations of enemies, or modifiers on certain randomly-generated bosses, can be a bit unfair or frustrating (or at least feel that way). They are fairly rare though. Example: shielded kamibots, or a boss with heal, damage reflect, shield and super teleport.
In it's current state, I highly recommend this game.  As a bonus, the developers are still adding to this game. They also read the suggestions people make in the discussions, so hopefully over time the list of things I don't like will shrink!
If anyone disagrees with anything I've said here, or any information is outdated/irrelevant, please leave a comment.

Many people said here about bugs, controls, problems, etc. Earlier I had original CD and what I can say, that there always were some problems with it; as I've heard, earlier developers have lost workdata of this game and couldn't fix many things by then. There were some fan-fixes, but still they've couldn't fix all. In many cases game haven't worked at all. There were no background music, chashes on a map change, control freezes. Now I see that the Steam team and community is really working on it, trying to make things better. And they really doing things better — the issue with background music (wich simply haven't worked on a platforms higher than Win2000) now is solved and gone. For now they've really solved many old issues. All works fine. Earlier I've played and passed all it through on Windows 2000 (for the original version of the game it looks like the only OS with wich The I of The Dragon works without any problems at all), Windows XP (haven't worked at all without serious manipulations, at least in my case neither I, nor my friends couldn't fix it and launch — it was completely broken), Windows 7 (worked fine but without music, hehe; sometimes had a control freezes). This version I've tired on Windows 8; I haven't play it long for now, mostly for testing, though, but by this time I haven't found any really serious issues, if not count one with startup-video that plays souns but has black screen instead the video. But with comparison with all other what was with it earlier... it's a complete minor.
And by that time were lack of guides about how you can fix all these problems; earlier at some problems were no answers at all; now It was surprisingly to find there many of them here, on steam + support. I think, with some time and one day they'll fix last serious issues with it.
For now, you will probably need to deal with having some technical issues, but known bug fixes now you can find in the community guides. Earlier, many years ago, there was NONE of that.
About controls; some said that you will need all of the keyboard + complete mouse, but it is a little not fair. Controls really can be a little bit complicated before you get used to them, because you'll need many keys for MAGIC (numbers, and, if I remember correctly, F-s), but basically what you'll really need for comfortable game — arrows on keyboard, maybe WASD, tab, left shift and space + one or two keys for aim. And a map. And that's all. More or less controls of an old standart for two hands; you'll need mouse only to change angle of a view (or set this separately on keyboard) or aim on enemy on wich dragon doesn't aim automatically by some reasons (usually landscape's specs). You can change all the keys (now it is working, at least on Win8x64 — earlier it worked only on Win2000, at least for me), and with some experiments find the comfortable control settings of your own.
Back in the original version there already were normal controls set. Now you'll maybe need to find a fine settings by your own by playing with them for some time, but that's not such an awful thing.
Also you can TRY to set gameplay mostly on the mouse, but this, in my opinion, is a harder way.
All other playing and upgrade system is pretty easy understandable; as a serious cons I can say only that the game really may be linear and monotonic for modern players since gameplay by itself is simple without many-many things to do and can become boring. But it's ok if play it with some pauses between. You will need to build cities and sometimes to protect them. Beat the monsters. You can't land your dragon since he's prisoned to be forever in the air, but...
There
, and they're pretty hard. Mostly after them is such a happyness to get back in the air. =)
But no sidequests and things like that. It's just a linear story and the enemies. And views around...
You will have 3 different dragons at choice: red (fire one) is the easiest to play since he's the strongest both magically and phisically. Blue (ice) is the most beautiful of them, but also this one is the hardest way to beat the game, since he's pretty weak but good at magic... but at a
; from the start it can be difficult to play with him, also further you will find many difficulties because of his specs. But he's interesting. Challenging in many ways, but still my favorite. Acid one is something between them both, but also has his moments. And also not so easy one to play with. You will "raise" your dragon all game long, making him stronger, adding abilities-spells.
Also overall difficulcy of the game can be changed.
Graphycs were amazing back then and even now, when it counts as pretty aged, it is still way more beautiful than in many other modern 3D games, especially if count its not so high price. It is simply beautiful; the overall design, the landscapes. Dragon's moves seems anatomicaly realistic. You'll also have a change of a daytime by day/night/sunset/sunrise! With all the lights and colors. And it came from 2004! Many nowadays games don't have such a beauty.
Another thing, that I've actually disliked a bit, is the change of an original soundtrack. I'm still keeping the records from original CD and now thinking that that first OST is still fitting more to all this, but maybe there were reasons to change it, also as with the language.
Well, I think I've said enough already — back ago I've played much time in it and still have nostalgic feelings about it. Maybe I'll have some time to replay it fully now. I had original Russian version and it also feels a little weird that here is no original language, but it will be interesting to play in it on English. Something new. =)
Good luck with work on it, guys; and real thanks for this release and all the effort you've already had put into it.

Homebrew is one of those games that once you get going, you can't stop (evident by my 900+ hours and climbing.) Put simply: Homebrew is a vehicle builder where the only limitation is  your determination and imagination!
There's definately a pretty steep learning curve concerning some of the build aspects and the logic in Homebrew. But, if you ever get stuck Homebrew has an incredible community where more than a few people are more than willing to lend a hand. Then, once you get past the learning curve Homebrew becomes this marvelous game where you can push your creativity, imagination, and knowledge to create some beautiful vehicles (or buildings) and then make it work with all the bells and whistles.
When you build, it's entirely up to you when to say enough features is enough for one vehicle, from the simple forward/back, left/right car to a jet that can take off and land on its own to a rocket (or other vehicle) that can take off, fly somewhere, return and land! The best part: these are just three examples I came up with on the fly and by no means guidlines for any vehicle nor are they suggestions to how simple that vehicle might be. I.E.: that "simple" car I described might actually be the most complex thing you've ever built because it has active aerodynamics, steering assist, an automatic gearbox you made yourself, and so much more!
In addition to Homebrew's top notch builder, you can enjoy your vehicles in multiplayer with everyone else and their vehicles! From simple car shows or "knowledge swaps" to races organized by the community to build contests (also organized by the community) there's very rarely no one on Homebrew's official servers.
In all, Homebrew is a wonderful game that I highly recomend to anyone looking to build the cars, motorcycles, helicopters, planes, rockets, airships, boats, subs, etc. of their dreams while challenging themselves with finding the perfect shape or successfully completing a logic system.
It's also the best feeling when something you've been trying to get to work after days of hair ripping, tear jerking, blood losing frustrations starts working perfectly.

Since i've racked 700 hours of game time now I thought it'd already be time to write a review.
TL;DR amazing game, has its issues like any other alpha game but despite those has a lot going for it.
As you can guess from the title, Homebrew is about building vehicles and other creations. Despite being often compared to Scrap Mechanic I find that comparison injustified as Homebrew is vastly different.
The core of Homebrew is building vehicles. The tools give to you are very powerful. I've yet to come across any other vehicle building game that allows this much freedom and accuraccy. Pipes and plates are what makes up the frame and body of the vehicle and on that you attach other parts. Tuner is where you make your vehicle work. Tuner system is really powerful tool, you can even make simple video games with it and all that in easy to use graphical interface. You don't need any sort of programming skills to make cool stuff with it but it can still be a bit hard for beginners to get a grasp of. You can create truly amazing stuff in this game and quite complex mechanisms too. The biggest problem builder has right now is that it is a bit slow to use due to variety of reasons.
Development is going strong. Devs are not making the game just to make money, they are truly passionate about it. They are a really cool group of people and regularly interact with the community. They really listen to us players and our feedback.
One of the best parts of the game is the community. The community is small but really friendly and helpful. People gladly help anyone with a problem they are having with their vehicle. Community mainly interacts thorugh Homebrew's own Discord server, it's like an extension of the game itself. This is truly the most awesome game community i've ever come across.
Homebrew isn't without its problems though. Currently there's no goal in the game, just a sandbox, but its definitely going to be fixed in the future. The game is still in Alpha meaning many features are not in the game, complete or are subject to change. Physics do need a bit of refinement here and there. The game can be overwhelming for new players, the learning curve is steep but it is being worked on.
Homebrew is truly an unique game. Despite its flaws it became my favourite game almost instantly after i bought it. If you can come over the usual issues with Early Access Alpha games there is an amazing game and awesome community to be found here. If you like creative games and designing vehicles, Hombrew is definitely a strong recommendation from me.

As the old saying goes, "Stealth is optional for this mission."  This is very true for Echo, and you can most certainly try, but you're gonna have a very bad time.  Ultra Ultra has crafted a gorgeous, albeit simple game with a straightforward hook: your enemies can only do what you do.  En has all the classic moves of other stealth games; she can crouch and sneak, sprint and vault over obstacles, make distractions, (to include playing musical instruments) and she can of course choke people out or shoot them.  You may be tempted to use the full arsenal of your abilities as other games have trained you, but then so do the echoes, and one echo jogging after you may be fine, but when there's three of them and one of them is throwing something and another is firing off her riot gun things are quite different.  The first time an echo jumped up from a crouch and sprinted at me I was so surprised I almost died immediately.  Ultimately, you have to make decisions on whether or not to use your *very* limited firearm, utilize your surroundings or time  your actions so that you can weave your way through their patrols unseen and give them no new weapons to use against you in the next cycle.
The two characters, En and the disembodied voice of her AI companion reflect on her history and her purpose as she navigates this planetwide labyrinth and you find yourself after a while genuinely caring about the two.  The game is actually quite short, which is probably a good thing, because the simple and repetetive game mechanics could only keep your attention for so long.  Your missions, environment aside, come in three primary flavors: Get to the waypoint, collect two keys on opposite sides of a long hallway to open a door, or collect glowing orbs across a vast room to unlock a gate to the next area.  It's simple, basic really, but still fun.
All in all I found this to be quite an enjoyable game.  There were moments of joy, moments of frustration, and while I wouldn't call this game scary, there were very intense moments of me desperately trying to stay alive and running for my life into pitch black corridors.  Feel free to check out my playthrough at
, but really I'd recommend you play it yourself!

I'm going to, very tentatively, positively recommend this game. The first thing I should say is: if you're going to play it, do it in short bursts at a time. This is not the kind of game you'll enjoy if you play it for 2+ hours at a time (like I did). It will wear on you very quickly. This is the kind of game you should play if you want something to do for an hour or so. The game is about 8 hours total.
The core mechanic of the game is pretty solid - part of what makes it interesting is deciding which actions the AI learns or unlearns in each cycle, deciding which things you can afford to let the AI do that won't hinder your own progress, etc. Unfortunately after a while it does start to become "do as little as possible while the lights are on, then go ham during the blackouts." The biggest issue that I have with this mechanic, though, is that it's the ONLY thing this game has going for it. There really aren't any other mechanics. They change it up once, late game, and it's for the shortest amount of time they could possibly muster. It isn't even really for gameplay purposes, it's for narrative.
That's the main issue I have with this game overall - it's very shallow. You have the central mechanic of the ligh-dark cycles. You have the one art-deco type scenery (with the maintenence areas in between where they dump all the exposition). The game feels too structured - you figure out the pattern to the gameplay after a while, which makes playing it for extended periods of time really torturous.
The levels are beautiful - seriously, any part of this game could be used as a wallpaper. I spent a pretty long time gawking at the scenery, even after I figured out all the levels are just recolors of the other ones. The biggest problem with them is they're big. WAY too big. Literally bigger than they could possibly need to be. It seems sometimes the devs were more concerned about the spectacle of a hallway that goes on forever than making smaller levels with something to do in them other than smack some big tuning forks and collect glowing orbs. It makes completing the 2 kinds of objectives in this game more of a chore than they need to be. Combine the gigantic level size with the constantly respawning enemies and the extremely scarce save locations and you're in for a hard time. At some points I felt like they could have cut out a huge chunk of the middle of the game, simply because so little changes from level to level that it felt like I wasn't making any progress at all.
Side note - the save location stuff is infuriating. Having to backtrack and risk dying to enemies that you already killed only to lose all the progress you made was the worst part of this game for me. You can't have players roaming around a football-field-sized level collecting 50 goddamn orbs and not let them save whenever they want. It feels like it was done that way on purpose to pad out gameplay time. This feeling comes up a lot - especially in the sections in between gameplay levels, where they force you to walk the entire time while you listen to En and London have an argument.
That said, despite all the cons, I still had a fun time with the game. There are certain times where the scenery of this game is really incredible. The story was interesting - it wasn't necessarily anything special but I liked hearing tidbits about the world En lives in. I just wish they had talked about it MORE and not just in between gameplay sections. As mentioned before, the central mechanic is still fun and interesting. You get a sense you're learning the patterns and when you work out a system it's rewarding until it starts to feel repetetive. Again, if they had just done MORE with it I'd have even better things to say.
As negative as this review is, I would still recommend the game. To me it's a fun thing you can play for a little while. It's got a great style and visuals, and an interesting premise, but I just wish THEY HAD DONE MORE WITH IT.

Echo is a short game and I'll keep this review short too:
Pros
+ The atmosphere is equal parts sci-fi wonder and empty church creepy
+ The cycle mechanic works fairly well if you decide to play along with it
+ The story and voice acting is really well done
+ The backdrop of the story is well made (envrions, surrounding plot, the details)
Cons
- Very minimal enemy type variance and ability variance limits the variation in player interactions
- Some interesting concepts (using Echoes as tools during certain stretches) aren't fleshed out well
- While the story is short the repetitive nature of the puzzle types can drag on
- This is a stealth game where the hiding mechancis aren't good
I truly believe that there are going to be a lot of people that enjoy this game for the atmosphere and the story, but if you're buying this for the stealth mechanics then I'd tell you to look elsewhere. This is at its core an atmospheric game designed to make you feel, and while it does a good job of inspiring awe and trepidation it does a somewhat bad job of making the base stealth fun.
All in all: Stealth fan? Only buy if you are into a good story. General Player? With a bit of patience this could be a gem.

There seems to be 16 levels and in the first 9 a new unit or spell is given. The mechanics of the game is very simple summon troops to push back the computer's troops and attack its castle. The troops the player may use can either stand by the player's castle and shoot projectiles or the unit may walk to toward the computer's castle to attack and push back the enemy troop. The warrior and archer are the default units for the attacks. The axeman and wizard are like defaults but stronger and slower. The player may use spells to heal their own troops, attack enemy troops, or freeze them. The player has access to 4 spells but really 3 of them do different things. The fire and lighting spell are used to attack the enemy troops. The ice freezes them. The green light heals your own. The player gets one at a time as the the advance through the level. At level 9 the player gets a screen clearing dragon to breath fire on the enemies. The units and spells can be upgraded with coins that are won after beating each level. Although these coins cannot be farmed, upgrades can reset and the player may put it in where the want it. The game would be fine if not for the bugs and a balancing issue.
The computer seems to have a faster cooldown which allows it to summon more troops and use more spells then the player making the game into a boring game of tug o war in the later levels. Also in the later levels spells might not activate when you click them which makes it easy for the computer to kill your troops and prolong the level. In level 9 there is a bug where the UI may disappear and reappear. When the UI disappears the player may not use their spells or summon troops but the computer can since it does not need the UI. Even when the UI stops going off and on the ability to summon troops is gone making the level unwinnable. That was the only game breaking bug in the game that I encountered. But there are some other things that make the game bad. The sound tracks only has 3 songs one for the battle, one for the level select, and one for the upgrades. This would not be so bad if the levels did not take so long or if the player could mute ingame. The animations for spells is sometimes delayed from activation. But the animation fro the units are always delayed when the are fighting each other, sometimes it takes a full second for the unit to do the attack animation andfor the oppenent to react.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Kill to Collect is a single- and multi-player 'rogue-lite' action game in a dystopian cyberpunk setting.
You play one of four bounty hunters who spend their time delving into the deeper floors of Earth's last city, Geoshelter Alpha, in search of their prey. And when they find them? Well, they kill to collect, obviously!
Graphics - The graphics all have a great cyberpunk-like feel to them, with dark backgrounds combined with bright neon and flashy weapon effects, and the character outfits, while mostly looking a little silly, fit the atmosphere well. Enemies are a little bit boring and samey across some levels, and are basically made up from two groups: robots and humans.
The graphics are a little small, though, and with no zooming available to focus in on the action, I found it difficult with some enemy models to see the animations clearly enough to predict their attack timings.
Graphics options include the usual detail level, full screen / window mode, and resolution settings, as well as a number of advanced features like SSAO, bloom, and antialiasing. I played in full HD with everything set to maximum and experienced no problems on an aging gaming laptop (485m video card), but others have reported some issues on much newer hardware. The developer is looking into it, but from my point of view, it runs like a dream!
Sound - Music is nice enough: a sort of heavy rock-type beat with electronic melodies. In any case, it fits the game well and doesn't get in the way. Sound effects are similarly good.
Gameplay - The game has three different gameplay options, each able to be played in single player mode or cooperatively with up to three other people: Story Mode (a campaign, including a minimal tutorial), Challenge (fight your way through eight levels as quickly as possible), and Free Hunt (do any bounty, without the story mode's extra story bits). Ultimately, though, each mode boils down to the same thing for each level: descend to a lower floor of the city and fight your way through room after room of bad guys until you come to the boss: your target. Then collect your bounty.
The game structure within each bounty takes a room-by-room approach that is similar to other games such as the Binding of Isaac, although with none of the unique encounters of that game. Each floor consists of a number of isolated rooms, and enemies from one room can't travel to another. You progress by wiping out all the enemies in a room, after which you can unlock the door to a connecting room and do it all again. You're rewarded on completion of each room with 'tech', one of the game's two currencies, and you receive a bonus if you complete a room without getting hit by an enemy. When you reach the final room of the level you're awarded some food stamps, the other currency, and can then spend your tech and food stamps on random items that only last until the end of the current bounty.
Occasionally you'll find chests in some of the battle rooms, which can be opened to reveal random one-use items or temporary weapons. These are fairly few and far between though, and are usually (always) found in 'challenge rooms': rooms with a much higher number of enemies than normal rooms. Upon completing one of these rooms you can open the chest and grab the loot inside.
When you complete a bounty -- and also if you fail at it -- you receive a reward for the number of kills you made through the level, with a bonus for killing the bounty target. This then adds to your progress in various 'loadouts' (equipment with which you can begin a level), titles (simply a name), and outfits for your hunters. There is thus some limited customisation and progression available, but it's a hard slog for what seems like not quite enough of a reward.
It's fun to play, although it is more frustrating than it should be, as dying in single-player mode seems to take you all the way back to the start of the first floor of the bounty, even if you've reached one of the end-floor rooms that is supposed to respawn you there. Because of this it took me over an hour of play just to finish the first proper bounty after the tutorial, because I had to do the whole thing about seven times.
A few niggly issues brought the game down a bit, though. For starters, the game is essentially a twin-stick shooter using left hand on the keyboard for movement and right hand on mouse for aiming and shooting. But the default keyboard and mouse controls just don't work in a frantic situation, as they make it impossible to use items like medkits. Unfortunately it's not very easy to make it better with the choices available for keyboard configuration, either; I've only managed to improve it slightly by mapping the middle mouse button. The game does claim to have full controller support, which would probably work much better. I haven't had a chance to test that yet, though. The mouse aiming also sometimes doesn't work quite right, leaving your character swinging off at some weird angle well away from the direction of the mouse pointer. The lobby and menu interface is also a little quirky, with a bit of searching required in order to work out how to activate or use any rewards you win.
The story in the game is enjoyable, if a little derivative, but the text really needs a bit more attention. There are some very awkwardly worded sentences that just don't flow well, and numerous grammatical errors as well. The four characters all have different background stories and in-game abilities, but without extra characters to open up or more customisation and progression available, it feels like it's not quite enough.
I say Kill to Collect is a 'rogue-lite' game as it includes random dungeon generation, and some degree of random drops (although in this case they're not enemy drops, but rather sporadic chests and end-of-floor shops with random equipment), but it doesn't include any of the mega-loot options like a true rogue-like game. There is only very limited character modification available, and mostly only temporary progression.
Pros:
+ A great atmosphere; a good cyberpunk feel
+ It's great fun most of the time
+ Single player and cooperative multiplayer
+ Achievements
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- Keyboard and mouse controls don't work well in frantic situations, which are common
- It's very frustrating sometimes
- Most character upgrades are only temporary; a permanent upgrade tree would be a fantastic addition
- No one in multiplayer yet
Re-reading this review it looks as though I'm being a bit down on Kill to Collect, but that's just because it's almost fantastic; it just misses out due to those little niggles I mentioned.
But it is still a very good fun game. I highly recommend it.

I've a lot of respect for the devs who clearly put a metric♥♥♥♥♥♥tonne of work into remaking Master of Magic, but the apple has fallen flat. I'd suggest trying a similar original game, or just grab MOM on GOG for a few bucks - seems in this case you really can't beat a classic.

On the bright side, this is a Master of Magic remake that captures some of the spirit of the original and expands on it in a way that respects some of the qualities of the original. It improves some flaws of the original, and retains some.
On the dark side, the map UI is very messy. This seems to be again a victim of the "more polygons = better graphics" school of graphic design, while it should be clear by now that that needn't be the case. The overland map is still essentially 2d, so 3d graphics do not belong there, they simply make it harder to tell things apart, which is a crucial problem for strategy games. There you want a lot of information unambiguously accessible without clutter. Keep the 3d for games that actually play in 3d. For strategy gaming I want clear icons that tell me what is going on, not units that got animated down to their shoelaces. Don't waste money and time on that, fix the bugs instead.
So I give some cautious support, but be aware that this is far from a finished game still and as such that should reflect the price you're willing to pay for it.
