If you’ve ever played Geometry Dash you’ll feel right at home with Dashy Square as the gameplay is inspired by it and feels very similar. The idea is simply you must navigate your way to the end of each level past the various objects you’ll encounter. If you have little patience or hate cheap deaths then this game isn’t for you because without lightning fast reflexes you’ll be dying a lot; Dashy Square is HARD.
You constantly move through the level and must jump, slow yourself down, fly and dodge your way past the objects that’ll appear in front of you as you move. The level will often bounce, flip or disappear as you play so focus is a must! Each level is different and they continuously get harder even though the ‘Easy’ levels are pretty hard themselves but you can practice each level without the fear of dying if you’re really struggling.
Each level is nicely designed and very colourful and there are a total of 16 levels currently with more coming soon so there is a nice amount of content for the price.
Dashy Square is a fairly fast paced game with a soundtrack to match each and every level which I love. I had hoped to purchase the soundtrack via Steam after playing but this isn’t an option which is a shame. There is a link in game to the soundtrack in-game where I think some of the tracks are downloadable but it is still something i’d like to see on Steam so I could easily use the tracks in other platformers that allow audio import.
There is also a nice amount of visual customization in game from all the textures of powerups and the in level background, to how your avatar looks and even the colour of the trail your produce from items. You can also choose your practice, menu and victory songs. The combination of these two stops the visuals and sound becoming repetitive and increases the replayability. You also have a massive assortment of achievements to get as well meaning even once you’ve completed all the levels there is still stuff you can do.
The game has a few cons, some levels are uncompletable without dying at least once or playing practice mode first. I’m all for difficult levels and a nice challenge but some of the deaths are unavoidable without prior knowledge of what is to come. This makes replaying a level again that you would have otherwise completed a little annoying. The only other issue is the game can seem a bit confusing first because none of the menus really explain what they do but it’ll come to you very quickly.

Dashy square is a  fun to play clever methodical indie action  game. Its for those who have fast reflexes and have littile or no time to play lengthy indie action games. But be not mistaken , its not any action  game, its better. Here you methodically dodge obstacles instead of blowing them to bits. As they say -The best offence is a good defence.
Its a colorful game with 16 levels with great and varied music and gameplay. Every level is almost new in content. There are five levels with waves. The game is based on a directional algorithm whose only purpose is to entertain. Even though 2d in orientation. You face seemingly different obstacles with varied difficulties. The music is actually designed to help players overcome these obstacles.
The obstacles are some designed to be jumped over , some to be flyed over,  yet some to be paused for.There are various tools ingame like the teleporter which only changes the location/height  of the player, there are some boxes which are chained, they  fall after regular intervals. Some boxes are orchestrated in such a way that you must fly over them. Even some passages are designed to increase or decrease the players momentum.
Like wise there are tools provided to the player which enable the player to jump or fly. The basic mechanics of the game is simple it trys to introduce new  obstacles killing monotony of repeating a level, while it plays on directional orientations of the user within the limitations of the two dimensional computer screen.The game plays on every usable sense available to a general player, namely direction speed, audio. what more there’s a level editor coming soon which is designed to hopefully broaden the players experience even more.
In terms of creativity the games architect sulejmani has not only outdone himself but left room for the community as well.It may look similar to  certain games  (unmentioned here) but it really isn’t.There are many pros to this game and relatively no cons. But to mention a few
PROS
+ the levels are fun,varied and interesting
+The game is pocket friendly at onlt $ 3 or so
+The game has innovative music
+ the game play is smooth
+level editor (soon to come)
CONS
-The music is a bit too loud
-The spatial flow of the game can be nauseating at times  and can cause a headache if not gotten used to fast.
All in all it’s a 8/10 game. The game was released on 26th April by Sulejmani. The steam version is in  five languages  till date English,Spanish,Italian,French,Portugese. It comes with steam trading cards and steam achievements

A few days ago I was talking a friend and he had said that "[Sol Survivor] is the pinnacle of tower defense games" or something to that effect...and I have to agree with him. Most would say PvZ, Dungeon Defenders, or Defense Grid, but I really think if most people gave this game a shot they would see where I'm coming from. It's a seemingly simple game, that is more complex than meets the eye, there are many strategies to play around with and it's an amazing learning process, you master the game only through playing around with different builds. Even at 100+ hours I'm still coming up with tweaks to my best strategies, as well as coming up with new bizarre ones that somehow work. Although it's nearly 5 year olds it only shows it's age visually and remains the best true tower defense game I have ever played and I consider myself a tower defense junkie.
The basics of this game is to place turrets around the paths of the enemies (which is already determined and easy to pick out on the map). Most turrets have pretty good range, so it's easy to make a good choke. Sounds simple, yet surprisingly there is a lot you can do. There is a fairly good variety of turrets and each of them specialize in something, making them all valuable in some way (or you can at least incorporate them all into some solid strategy). It takes time and playing around to really learn the ins and out of each turret. A lot of information is included in the in-game encyclopedia, but even that isn't completely exhaustive. On top of damaging turrets there are also a slew of support turrets that also mix up how you strategize placement and spending priorities. (note: money is gained in-game in different ways depending on what the income setting is set on) Another element of gameplay is the powers, your character has 100 max power. You can only choose so many powers and towers (I want to say about 8 each) every time you play a map, so that's another aspect you have to strategize. Regardless of you what you pick you'll be limited to casting your abilities based on how much power you have, it regenerates over time like mana would, so using your powers efficiently and at critical times is key.
One argument could be made against my assertion that this is perhaps the best tower defense out there and that is it doesn't feature path building. That's to say you can't influence the path an enemy takes or build constructions, something that is key in games like Sanctum, Orcs Must Die!, and Defense Grid. Admittedly the ability to structure enemy pathing really adds to the strategizing process. At the same time, it can also make it easier (leading orcs to one solidified choke is key in OMD, and in DG the only way to get on the top 10 leaderboards is to bounce enemies back and forth blocking and unblocking sections of your structures), so it's arguable about what's better, I definitely like path building, but even so Sol Survivor still somehow captivates me more than games that allow for that.
I think this is due in part to how relaxing and inviting this game is. There is never a time where I don't feel like playing this, that I'm not in the mood. The game is very laid back, the soundtrack is quite ambient, a lot of the levels are nighttime or snowy levels which means a lot of cool colours (grays and blues). The enemies move a nice constant rate, they aren't ferocious or in your face as they are in games like Sanctum or Orcs Must Die. As mentioned before you do have powers (abilities) but also mentioned before you can't spam them so even the "combat" aspect of the game is laid back. Overall it's a great game to kick back to, especially if you're with friends since you can spend most of the time chatting, both strategizing with each other and just talking about whatever strikes your fancy.
This game has a good chunk of content, and playing survival in particular has yet to get old. I've played the campaign with friends quite a few times and still always enjoy replaying it. The difficulties are well balanced, you won't be mastering the hardest difficulty anytime soon, and since the survival mode is endless (and it gets exponentially harder) there is never a skill cap where you can essentially "beat" the survival mode. I don't feel like I've said enough about one of the games I love the most, but I'll wrap up by saying if you want a good tower defense game with focus on tower placement and a less active combat role then look into Sol Survivor, and if you're serious about trying it, find some friends you like playing and nag them to play with you, since friends really do make this game even greater than it already is (or ask me).

I'm genuinely fond of this little game. It tries its very best to provide an entertaining story campaign for you to go through, and it mostly succeeds, provided you don't hate its sense of humour - which may just be trying too hard here and there. I enjoyed it anyway, mainly because I can appreciate calling a card "Roast Duck" and making it actually useful.
You could of course fast track through the story bits, but that would leave you playing a very simplistic deckbuilding game with the lightest of rpg elements, and one that's not brilliantly balanced to boot. You become OP very fast and, if you spend your card money well from the start, combat is never going to be a challenge. Some cards are simply overpowered and completely overshadow all the rest. Most unit skills are also very underwhelming, with the exception of attack buffs. And once you're decently set up, there is never a need to alter your deck to deal with different types of enemies: You get one decent enough attack unit with a bit of HP padding, use your two other units to buff it up or debuff the oponents, rinse, repeat. Thankfully the game doesn't resort to damage sponge enemies, so the combat never overstays its welcome.
So you follow your streamlined quest, travel around the map, talk to people, dwarves, elves and monkeys, do some arena combat for extra cash, solve riddles, look around for hidden stashes, do some (not terribly interesting or effective) levelling up, and before you know it the game is over. You can keep playing arena fights after finishing the story if you want, but you probably won't.
I don't make it sound all that great, do I? I did very much enjoy myself though. Everything is solidly polished, I liked the "oldfashioned" art style, the music was enjoyable, the story never became too silly to bother with, and the casual difficulty level made it a fun distraction for lazy evenings. Just don't come here looking for a challenging deck builder. Northmark is the quintessential "good for what it is" game, and that's perfectly fine by me.

Most modern adventure games disappoint me. I miss games like monkey island 1 and 2, or space quest (especially 5). I was a kickstarter backer of HM Spiffing. I refused to play the demo, waiting for the full game. And every time I've thought about this game, I've worried it would disappoint me to. Clearly I have nothing to worry about.
Every other adventure game I've played that's come out in the last few years has lacked 1 thing or another that is an important part of what makes these games great. HM Spiffing missed nothing. The humour is great. Every puzzle actually has logical reasoning behind it, as opposed to just having to try random stuff to reach a solution. The story is top notch, the graphics and score are great. It's a fairly short game--It took me about 2 days. But, it has a full good story and it leaves you wanting more. I wish it was longer, and I think the developer does too--they have already been talking about an episode 2. But it is amazing. If this is a genre you love, even if you feel like newer games have been failing to be what you want from the genre, go give this one a try. You will not be disappointed.
P.S. explore the options menu.... It has at least 1 hidden joke in it.

Her Majesty’s SPIFFING is a short, but very good point and click adventure game with funny dialog and amusing characters.
You are part of a two man crew searching for a habitable planet to colonize on behalf of Great Britain. The story is cute, and silly. I was satisfied with the ending, but it definitely leaves the story open for a sequel. The dialog is full of witty banter, and has a whole lot of puns that made me smile several times during my playthrough. The game makes many references to outdated real world things and other games, which I found to be quite funny. Does anyone else remember clippy, and how cute, but annoying he was?
The point and click gameplay was as expected. You click around to move, and choose what you want to interact with, and then decide how you want to try and interact with it. The puzzles are clear-cut; they don’t offer much of a challenge, and the game even acknowledges that fact. Movement felt on par with other point and click adventure games I’ve played, like Sam & Max. The character usually cooperates, but sometimes when the camera angle change it causes you to walk the wrong way.
Overall, I enjoyed the game, especially all the witty banter, and out of game references that came along with it. It’s a good pickup for those who enjoyed Sam & Max or Tales of Monkey Island. Although, it is an extremely short game, so you may want wait for a sale.

This is a game that is far more obviously the child of Master of Magic than many recent games have claimed. The ideas, rules, races and structure of the game could all happily have sat in the classic MoM - a fantasy based 4x game with a hugely nostalgic following, and rightly so. What that game did so wel - endless discovery even after dozens of hours, multiple ways to play, a huge depth of content - it really was a joy to play even years after all the graphics had become terribly dated.
So Planar Conquest, by sticking so closely to the model has every reason to be a highly enjoyable game. Yet it isn't. In reality there is no one thing that makes it fall over - each individual element, from discoveries to make, races to play and spells to cast is there, yet the sum of it all is so very curiously flat. The UI is pretty aweful and very 'sticky' - by which I mean everything moves about in such a reluctant fashion, as if it needs a push. On top of this the unit icons are all way to complex for the size they are, making them all largely indistinguishable after hours of play, and then when combat comes (which is probably the best feature) it becomes hard to care about your units because they all look rather indistinct (even once you have learned how to move the combat map around, which is of course not the same as in the strategic map) and are even more slow about responding to clicks, that in the end every battle becomes a chore. Autoresolve, for once, reflects fairly reasonably the results you'd get by doing the combat yourself, but apart from the risk of the occasional catastrophic loss of the hero, what is the point of skipping what should/might be the best part of the experience?
Ultimately it's hard to recommend this game even to die hard MoM fans.
What's it worth? £5 / $7

The building trees are about the same, there are less races, spells are organized by effect as well as by school, and there are heros. You can now play the previously disallowed combo life/death. Maintenance for death creatures has gone up. There are more planes. There are still bugs. In my case, lots of problems in the battle screen for example, recall hero doesn't always work, sometimes you cannot click the next button, and some spells seem to cause the game to freeze, but it looks like the developer is still actively supporting the game, so there will probably be patches. I would love this game if there were fewer bugs, but you can still have fun, just be prepared to sometime abandon a campaign and start over if the battles start locking up.
